findings.title: STALE_AFTER_SECONDS' rationale comment is now stale itself: it justifies the window by the exact silence the heartbeat exists to remove
findings.suggested_fix: Reword the comment on STALE_AFTER_SECONDS (lines 56-63). It still says the window is generous 'because a large conversion is legitimately quiet for minutes: progress is reported per stage, not per catchment' -- that was true when this issue existed, but the heartbeat now re-stamps every heartbeat_seconds() throughout a stage, so a working job is never quiet for more than a few beats. State the real remaining rationale (tolerance for missed/delayed beats, or how long a genuinely-dead job is left unreported) instead of the pre-fix justification.

findings.title: _replace's filesystem-backend check is redundant with its own except clause and over-broad in what it swallows
findings.suggested_fix: hasattr(backend, 'path') is effectively always true: Django's base Storage class defines path() (raising NotImplementedError) whether or not a concrete backend implements it, so the hasattr guard never actually filters anything -- the real discrimination is entirely the except clause underneath it. Worse, catching AttributeError inside that try, right after a hasattr check that supposedly confirmed the attribute exists, is contradictory and would silently swallow an unrelated bug inside a backend's path() implementation. Prefer either a direct predicate (isinstance(backend, FileSystemStorage)) or just `try: target = backend.path(key) except NotImplementedError: target = None`, dropping the hasattr wrapper and the ValueError/AttributeError catches unless there's a concrete backend that needs them.

findings.title: beat() has no guard around snapshot()/write_status, so a raising snapshot silently kills the heartbeat this commit exists to add
findings.suggested_fix: write_status() already catches broadly so 'a lost status update must not kill the job', but beat()'s loop calls snapshot() outside any try/except, and an uncaught exception in a thread just terminates that thread silently (default excepthook logs to stderr, nothing more). If any snapshot callable ever raises, the heartbeat stops for the rest of the stage with no warning in the job's own logging path, and the job goes back to looking dead after STALE_AFTER_SECONDS -- exactly the failure this commit fixes. Wrap the loop body in the same style of defensive try/except used for write_status, logging and continuing rather than exiting.

findings.title: The 'at' dict is mutated as two separate keys and read as two separate keys across a thread boundary, so a beat can observe a stage/message pair that never coexisted
findings.suggested_fix: say() does at.update(stage=stage, message=message) on the caller's thread while the heartbeat thread's snapshot lambda does (at['stage'], at['message']); each is two non-atomic dict operations, so a beat landing mid-update can pair a new stage with the previous message (or vice versa) in the status it writes. Store the pair behind a single key -- e.g. at['snapshot'] = (stage, message), read as at['snapshot'] -- so the shared state is one atomic dict access in each direction instead of two.

findings.title: _run is a generic name in a module whose other extracted helpers are already specific (_publish_directory, _upload_directory)
findings.suggested_fix: Rename _run to something that says what it runs, e.g. _run_stages or _run_pipeline -- 'run' is already overloaded everywhere else in this module as the noun (run_name, run_store, published run), and a bare verb _run reads as generic next to _publish_directory/_upload_directory. Keeping it a top-level function (rather than a closure inside publish) is justified by the tests monkeypatching ingest._run directly, so this is a naming fix only, not a shape change.

residual_risks: _replace writes via tempfile.mkstemp() then os.replace(); a SIGKILL landing between mkstemp and the replace/cleanup leaves an orphaned *.tmp file in the staging directory with nothing that ever sweeps it. Narrow window, but this system's whole premise is that jobs get OOM-killed, and the heartbeat multiplies the number of writes (and therefore windows) per job.
The dict shared between say() and the heartbeat's snapshot lambda ('at') is not lock-protected; see the P3 finding above for the specific race.
testing_gaps: No test exercises _replace's non-filesystem branch (backend.path() unavailable/raising), so the object-storage fallback to backend.save() and the hasattr/except discrimination are only exercised implicitly, not asserted.
No test covers a snapshot() (or write_status) failure inside beat() -- the silent-thread-death failure mode described in the P2 finding above is untested and would not be caught by the current suite.
No test asserts what happens if publish() raises inside _run while the heartbeat is mid-beat (e.g. a write racing the exception path) beyond the terminal-status ordering already covered.
